what: The confirmed findings of an independent attacking session against UTS, 2026-08-21. 73 attackers, 68 attacks landed, 67 reproduced under challenge. NONE of these were fixed — this is the evidence behind DEFECTS.md section 6.
howToRead: Each entry carries the attack, what was observed, what was expected instead, and how to reproduce it. A `correction` field, where present, is the attacker re-checking its own claim and narrowing it — read those before acting on the entry above them.
verifiedByHandInSession: The cross-site guard letting through a request whose Origin is the word "null" (reproduced: evil.example refused 403, "null" allowed 200 and disarmed).
The threshold tuner pricing at $0.125 a leg while the live signal path declares 0 (reproduced: on a near-fee edge the two pick 0.55 vs 0.50 and trade 38 vs 45 periods).
pinnedInTheStandingSuite: tests/adversarial/attack-http.js (the Origin sweep) and tests/adversarial/attack-engine.js (the money arithmetic).

confirmed.title: CSRF guard on the live-money controls fails OPEN for Origin: null (sandboxed-iframe / data: URL forgery)
confirmed.attack: POST /api/pilot/disarm (and /api/pilot/unhalt, /api/live/configs/:id/nuke, /api/live/configs/:id/deactivate, DELETE /api/live/setups/:id) with header 'Origin: null'. csrfGuard -> sameSiteOrNoBrowserOrigin() does `new URL('null')` which throws, sets host=null, and then `if (!host) return true` — the request is allowed. A real cross-site attacker page reaches this exact state with a sandboxed iframe (`<iframe sandbox>` auto-submitting a form) or a data:/file: document, both of which browsers send with Origin: null, while the owner's cached Basic Auth rides along.
confirmed.observed: Origin: null -> 200 {"ok":true,"request":{"armed":false,...}} (disarm succeeded); nuke -> 409 business error (guard passed, reached handler). Contrast Origin: https://evil.example -> 403 {"error":"cross-site request refused (CSRF guard on the live-money switch)"}. Same for 'Origin: not a url at all' (unparseable) -> 200, and 'Origin: file://' -> 200.
confirmed.expected: The module comment claims 'It only ever fails CLOSED on a positively cross-site browser request.' A sandboxed-iframe/data:-URL POST is positively cross-site AND carries Origin: null, so it must be refused (403), not allowed. The unparseable-Origin branch (`if (!host) return true`) breaks the stated guarantee. Note the ARM route is separately protected (requires application/json body + explicit {armed:true}, which cross-site HTML forms cannot send), so arming is not reachable this way — but disarm/unhalt/nuke/deactivate/delete are, and they ignore the body / accept any content type.
confirmed.reproduce:
cd <repo> && PORT=8531 node server.js &  # own port/data
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST -H 'Origin: null' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/pilot/disarm   # -> 200 (allowed)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/pilot/disarm  # -> 403 (refused)
confirmed.correction: The reported "nuke -> 409" was 404 in my run only because I used a non-existent config id; the guard-bypass (request reaches the handler) is identical either way. No effect on the finding, severity, or expectation. Everything else in the report reproduced exactly as described.

confirmed.title: purge accepts impossible / reversed keep-ranges and silently wipes the entire cache
confirmed.attack: POST /api/data/purge with a regex-valid but nonsensical month. The validator is only /^\d{4}-\d{2}$/, which accepts any month 00-99 and any year. Sending {"symbol":"BTCUSDT","keepFrom":"9999-99"} means 'keep months >= 9999-99', so every real month is below it and deleted. A reversed range {"keepFrom":"2025-01","keepTo":"2020-01"} (transposed from/to) also deletes everything.
confirmed.observed: {"symbol":"BTCUSDT","keepFrom":"9999-99"} -> 200 {"purged":11,"symbol":"BTCUSDT","kept":{"keepFrom":"9999-99","keepTo":null},...} (11 of 11 cache files deleted). {"keepFrom":"2025-01","keepTo":"2020-01"} -> 200 {"purged":11,...}. Also {"symbol":["BTCUSDT"]} (array) -> coerced to "BTCUSDT" and purged 11.
confirmed.expected: A destructive delete driven by a 'keep' instruction should validate that the month component is 01-12 and that keepFrom<=keepTo, and should refuse (or no-op) a range that would keep nothing. Right now a plausible typo in a KEEP field silently deletes the whole asset. This is exactly the project's stated danger class: a destructive op accepted on plausible-looking input, with no crash to notice it.
confirmed.reproduce: curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"symbol":"BTCUSDT","keepFrom":"9999-99"}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/data/purge   # -> purged:11 (everything)
confirmed.correction:
Three corrections; the finding stands but one item is inflated and two stronger consequences were missed.

1) DROP the array item. {"symbol":["BTCUSDT"]} with no keep range does exactly what the endpoint is documented to do and exactly what the "purge…" button already sends ({symbol} alone = whole asset). Coercion changes nothing. A multi-element array is rejected anyway: ["BTCUSDT","ETHUSDT"] -> "BTCUSDT,ETHUSDT" -> fails SYMBOL_RE (comma). Listing it as part of the attack overstates the finding.

2) "Silently wipes" overstates the aftermath in the TOTAL-wipe case. The response returns purged:13, the interface path prints "13 cached file(s) deleted" and redraws the table with the pair gone. A total wipe is loud. What is genuinely missing is refusal at the input and a confirm that states how much the range actually keeps.

3) The stronger case — the one that is genuinely silent and squarely in the project's danger class — is a PARTIAL wipe, which the report did not test:
   -d '{"symbol":"BTCUSDT","keepFrom":"2024-13","keepTo":"2026-07"}'
   -> 200 {"purged":11,"symbol":"BTCUSDT","kept":{"keepFrom":"2024-13","keepTo":"2026-07"},"planted":null}
   AFTER: 2 files (BTCUSDT-1h-2026-06.json, BTCUSDT-1h-2026-07.json)
   GET /api/data-state -> {"symbols":[{"symbol":"BTCUSDT","months":2,"from":"2026-06","to":"2026-07","toMonth":"2026-07","planted":false}]}
   Month 13 cannot exist, yet 11 of 13 months are gone and the pair still reports as a healthy pair with a shorter span. Nothing anywhere says the range was nonsense. Every later sweep then reads a truncated cache that looks fine — that is the plausible-wrong-answer failure, not the total wipe.

4) The reported count UNDER-REPORTS what was deleted. With fabricated-pair files present, purging the last real pair drives plantedSpan() to null and the route also unlinks every PLANTEDUSDT/PLANTEDLATEUSDT file (server.js:262-268). Observed with two stand-in planted files added:
   BEFORE: 15 files
   -d '{"symbol":"BTCUSDT","keepFrom":"9999-99"}' -> 200 {"purged":13,...,"planted":{"removed":true}}
   AFTER: 0 files
   15 files deleted, "purged":13 reported. So a typo in a KEEP field for a real pair also destroys the fabricated exam pairs, and the number on screen is wrong about how much went.

5) Note for the fix, not a defect on its own: /api/data/download (server.js:140) uses the same loose /^\d{4}-\d{2}$/ on startMonth/endMonth. It is non-destructive, but any month validator added should be shared.

confirmed.title: margin-floor (live liquidation guard) accepts arrays and hex strings as the risk number
confirmed.attack: POST /api/pilot/margin-floor with a non-number floor. The handler does `v = Number(raw)` after only rejecting when String(raw).trim()===''. Number([5])===5 and Number('0x10')===16, so an array or a hex string is silently accepted and written to data/pilot/margin-floor.json — the value the VPS sync carries to the box as the forced-liquidation brake.
confirmed.observed: {"floor":[5]} -> 200 {"ok":true,"marginFloor":{"floor":5,...}} (file written {"floor":5,...}). {"floor":"0x10"} -> 200 floor:16. {"floor":"1e3"} -> 1000. {"floor":" 2 "} -> 2. Empty POST (no body) -> 200 and clears the floor to null.
confirmed.expected: A live risk parameter must reject type-confused input. A JSON array is not a margin level; it should 400 like {"floor":"abc"} does (which is correctly refused). Accepting Number([5]) means a malformed or non-browser caller can set the liquidation brake from a value that was never a number the owner typed.
confirmed.reproduce:
curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"floor":[5]}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/pilot/margin-floor   # -> floor:5
curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"floor":"0x10"}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/pilot/margin-floor  # -> floor:16
confirmed.correction:
Three corrections — the finding is real but the report leads with the harmless half of it and overstates the attacker's reach.

1) THE LEAD EXAMPLES DO NOT PRODUCE A WRONG NUMBER; THE ONES IT MISSED REMOVE THE BRAKE. Number([5])===5, Number("0x10")===16, Number("1e3")===1000, Number(" 2 ")===2 all yield exactly the value the payload literally contained. That is sloppy input handling, not a wrong risk level. The dangerous member of the same family is on the other side of the same line — the blank test `String(raw).trim() === ''`. Any array that stringifies to empty passes it and is treated as "blank = clear the floor". Starting from a saved floor of 3, I observed:
  {"floor":[]}     -> 200 {"ok":true,"marginFloor":{"floor":null,...}}  file {"floor":null,...}
  {"floor":[null]} -> 200 floor:null
  {"floor":[[]]}   -> 200 floor:null
  {"floor":[""]}   -> 200 floor:null
So a JSON array — the exact type the report says should 400 — does not merely set a plausible number, it silently REMOVES the liquidation guard and answers ok. That is the "silently accepted, strictly weaker safety state" case, and it is the one worth putting in the title. (Also accepted, same family: "0b101"->5, "0o17"->15, "  +4  "->4, [[["7"]]]->7.)

2) THE EMPTY-BODY CLEAR IS THE DOCUMENTED CONTRACT, NOT A NEW BUG. The route's own error text says "or blank to clear", and public/trade.html:705 sends {floor:null} when the field is blank (behind a confirm dialog reading "Clear the margin floor?"). So no-body -> null is the intended blank path reached without an instruction. It is still a defect by this project's own standard — server.js:821-829 already fixed exactly this on /api/pilot/arm ("AN EMPTY REQUEST IS NOT A YES") and BUILD-PLAN.md:169-171 already records the same complaint against /api/pilot/stop-apply — but it should be reported as that known class, not as a fresh discovery.

3) SCOPE: NOT REACHABLE FROM A MALICIOUS WEB PAGE. The route is behind csrfGuard and it works — with `-H 'Origin: http://evil.example'` I got 403 {"error":"cross-site request refused (CSRF guard on the live-money switch)"}. Only a caller with no Origin/Referer (script/curl) gets through, because sameSiteOrNoBrowserOrigin fails open for those — itself already recorded in BUILD-PLAN.md against /api/pilot/arm. So the attacker is a local/non-browser caller or a buggy client, not a drive-by site.

Minor accuracy notes: {"floor":true} IS refused, but only incidentally — Number(true)===1 trips the "sits in the exchange's own liquidation range" check, not a type check; {"floor":{}} is refused ("[object Object]" -> NaN); {"floor":"Infinity"} refused. And the claim that this is "the value the VPS sync carries to the box" is not verifiable in this repo: the only in-repo readers of data/pilot/margin-floor.json are server.js:931/737 and lib/live/routes.js:80, both for showing "requested" beside what the box reports it is ENFORCING (which comes from the synced journal, lib/live/view.js:81). The carry is asserted in the comment at server.js:923-928; the sync itself lives outside this tree.

confirmed.title: clipUsd (per-trade dollar notional) has no upper bound and accepts arrays
confirmed.attack: clipUsd flows through greenlight shuttle, channel activate, and setup config update. validateOperational only checks `Number.isFinite(s.clipUsd) && s.clipUsd > 0` with no ceiling, and the routes pass Number(clipUsd) — Number([25])===25 and Number(1e308)===1e308. So an absurd position size, or an array, is accepted and stored as the trade notional (used by paper simulation now and live sizing at activation).
confirmed.observed: shuttle {"clipUsd":1e308} -> 200 setup.clipUsd:1e+308 (on disk clipUsd:1e+308). shuttle {"clipUsd":[25]} -> 200 clipUsd:25. config update {"clipUsd":1e308} -> 200 stored 1e+308.
confirmed.expected: A dollar position size should have a sane upper bound and reject non-number types, so a fat-finger / paste / malformed client cannot set a 1e308-dollar clip that reads as a believable number on screen. Contrast: clipUsd:0, -5, and "abc" are correctly refused; the gap is the missing ceiling and the array coercion.
confirmed.reproduce: curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"greenlightId":"<gl-id>","clipUsd":1e308}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/live/shuttle   # -> setup.clipUsd:1e+308
confirmed.correction: The defect is real; four corrections to the write-up. 1. "reads as a believable number on screen" is FALSE for 1e308. public/trade.html renders the clip at line 439 `$${Number(s.clipUsd).toFixed(0)}` and line 543 `${tile('Clip','clip','$'+Number(s.clipUsd).toFixed(0))}`. JS toFixed(0) goes exponential at >=1e21, so 1e308 prints "$1e+308" (verified: node -e 'Number(1e308).toFixed(0)' -> "1e+308"). That is loud, not plausible. 1e12 does print plainly ("$1000000000000") — still not believable. So the ceiling half of this finding is a missing-guard/data-integrity defect, not a plausible-wrong-answer defect. 2. The array claim is the weakest example of the real coercion hole and mis-states it as array-specific. `Number()` at routes.js:234 and :288 coerces ANY type, and [25] -> 25 preserves the intended value so nothing is silently wrong. The genuinely silent cases are the ones the report missed, all observed through /api/live/shuttle: {"clipUsd":true} -> 200 clipUsd=1 (a boolean becomes a $1 clip) {"clipUsd":"0x64"} -> 200 clipUsd=100 (hex string) {"clipUsd":"1e5"} -> 200 clipUsd=100000 {"clipUsd":" 25 "} -> 200 clipUsd=25 true->$1 and "0x64"->$100 are the doctrinal shape: a wrong number that looks entirely normal on screen. 3. The three doors do NOT behave alike. POST /api/live/setups/:id/config (routes.js:155-157) hands req.body straight to updateSetup with no Number(), so it REFUSES what shuttle/activate accept. Observed on the same setup: {"clipUsd":[25]} -> {"error":"clipUsd: must be a positive dollar notional"} and {"clipUsd":"50"} -> same refusal, while {"clipUsd":1e308} -> 200. Same field, same registry, two different rules for what a valid clip is depending on which door it comes through. That inconsistency is the more durable defect than the missing ceiling. 4. Escalation the report missed, which raises the ceiling half's severity: the box-side cap is derived from this same unbounded field. live-produce.js:31-40 builds the allowlist under the comment "The allowlist the box enforces (fail-closed there): exactly the configured clip — the box lets a setup trade at MOST what the owner configured, so a tampered intent upstream cannot resize it", with `max_clip_usd: s.clipUsd`. A 1e308 clip therefore sets the guard to 1e308 rather than being caught by it. (The executor itself, mx_executor.py, is not in this repo, so I cannot say what the box does with that number.) Two further things I observed, same root cause: 5. The other direction is silent and IS the plausible-wrong-answer shape. shuttle {"clipUsd":0.4} -> 200, stored 0.4; both render sites above print "$0" (node: Number(0.4).toFixed(0) === "0"). A book carrying a real 40-cent clip reads as zero clip on screen. Note public/trade.html:575 is `Clip $ ` — min=1 is a client-side hint only and line 620 reads the field with a bare `Number(...)`. 6. A REFUSED activation still leaves the bad value on disk. activate() shuttles first, then transitions, so my two rejected calls ("cannot go paper: cell.trailMult ... symbol BTCUSDT: target 'mx-1' serves [\"LTCUSDT\"]") still wrote setup-mt39m9wu-fa44f7.json with "clipUsd": 1e+308 and setup-mt39m9x5-75e958.json with "clipUsd": 777 (from {"clipUsd":[777]}), both state draft, channel paper/real. The 400 to the caller does not mean nothing was stored. Severity: keep it moderate, not high. No real order can result without keyRef plus the liveExecutable/target gate plus the arm switch, and 1e308 is visible. The parts worth fixing first are the type coercion at routes.js:234/288 (align the two doors with the config door, which already refuses non-numbers) and the "$0" render of a sub-dollar clip.

confirmed.title: stop-apply accepts an array as the live protective-stop fraction
confirmed.attack: POST /api/pilot/stop-apply with stopPct as a one-element array. The handler requires the key be present, then does `Number(raw)`; Number([0.11])===0.11, so the array passes every bound check (0<v<1, >=0.005 floor) and is written to data/pilot/fixed-stop.json as the live stop the sync carries to the box.
confirmed.observed: {"stopPct":[0.11]} -> 200 {"ok":true,"fixedStop":{"chosen":true,"stopPct":0.11,...}} (file {"stopPct":0.11,...}). Also {"why":12345} and {"why":["a","b"]} are silently dropped (typeof!=='string' -> why omitted) while stopPct is still applied.
confirmed.expected: stopPct should reject non-number types (array/object) rather than coerce them; a live risk parameter set from an array is the 'input accepted that should have been refused' failure. (stopPct:true, {v:..}, 0 and -0.5 are correctly refused — only the array slips through.)
confirmed.reproduce: curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"stopPct":[0.11]}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/pilot/stop-apply   # -> stopPct:0.11 written
confirmed.correction:
It reproduces, but the severity framing and one observation are wrong, and the report misses a strictly worse case in the same guard.

1) SEVERITY OVERSTATED — no wrong number is ever stored. Every array that gets through carries exactly one numeric element and is written as that same number (typeof "number", 0.11). Every array that is ambiguous or lossy is refused: [] -> Number 0 -> 400, [0.11,0.5] -> NaN -> 400, [[0.11]] -> the same 0.11 it contains. So this is not the project's "plausible wrong answer" failure — the record and the value the sync carries are correct and reproducible. It is loose typing, not a corrupted risk parameter.

2) IT GRANTS NO CAPABILITY THE CALLER LACKS. Only express.json is mounted (server.js:26 — no express.urlencoded), so a cross-site HTML form cannot reach this body parser at all, and csrfGuard/sameSiteOrNoBrowserOrigin refuses a cross-origin browser fetch. The interface never sends an array either: public/construct.js posts `Number($('#stopCustomPct').value)` (validated >0, <100, >=0.5 before posting), `Number(b.dataset.stop)` from the preset buttons, or literal null from "No stop (clear)". Anyone who can send [0.11] can send 0.11 — the coercion buys an attacker nothing.

3) ONE OBSERVATION IS WRONG. The report says {"why":12345} and {"why":["a","b"]} "are silently dropped ... while stopPct is still applied". Sent literally, with no stopPct key, both are REFUSED:
   curl -d '{"why":12345}' -> 400 {"error":"stopPct must be given explicitly — send a fraction to set a stop, or null to clear it. A request that says nothing is refused."}
   The drop only happens when stopPct is also present: {"stopPct":0.11,"why":12345} and {"stopPct":0.11,"why":["a","b"]} both -> 200 with "why":null.

4) THE SAME GUARD HAS A WORSE HOLE THE REPORT DID NOT REPORT: an empty string CLEARS a live protective stop. The condition is `if (raw != null && raw !== '')`, so "" skips every check and stores stopPct:null with chosen:true — the record then states the owner deliberately chose to run with no stop.
   After setting a real stop ({"stopPct":0.11,"why":"owner chose 11% after the sweep"} -> 200):
   curl -d '{"stopPct":"","why":"typed nothing"}' -> {"ok":true,"fixedStop":{"chosen":true,"why":"typed nothing","stopPct":null,...}}
   file: {"stopPct":null,"by":"owner","utc":"...","why":"typed nothing"}
   The comment directly above the handler says zero stays refused on purpose because "an empty box parses to 0, and a parse slip must not silently strip a live risk parameter" — but the literal wire value an empty box produces is "", and "" is treated as an explicit clear. That is the real "input accepted that should have been refused": it removes a live risk parameter and records the removal as a decision. (Current UI never sends "" — Number("")===0 is caught by construct.js before posting — so it is script-reachable only, same reachability as the array.)

Recommended framing if this is ever fixed (owner's call, not mine): reject non-number/non-null types outright (typeof check before Number), and treat "" the same as 0 — refused — rather than as a clear.

confirmed.title: inspect quorum is unbounded above the committee size and answers impossible questions with '0 trades'
confirmed.attack: GET /api/bracketlab/:id/inspect?file=...&quorum=999 (or 1e308, or negative). The route does `Number(req.query.quorum)||1` and inspectDump does `Math.max(1, Number(quorum)||1)` — there is no cap at the committee size. A 4-member committee asked for quorum 999 computes normally and reports zero trades and null pairwise agreement.
confirmed.observed: On a 4-member fixture: quorum=999 -> {"quorum":999,"committee":{"searchTrades":0,"holdTrades":0,...},"members":[...withTradeHold:null...]}. quorum=1e308 -> echoed quorum:1e+308, 0 trades. quorum=4 -> withTradeHold:1 for every member off just 2 hold trades. quorum=-5 and quorum=abc silently become 1.
confirmed.expected: A quorum above the committee size is impossible and should 400, not return '0 trades / no agreement' — which reads on screen as 'the committee never agreed' (a plausible wrong answer about the model) rather than 'you asked an impossible question'. The endpoint also echoes the absurd quorum back verbatim, cementing the false reading.
confirmed.reproduce: curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/bracketlab/<runid>/inspect?file=<dump>.json&quorum=999'   # -> committee.holdTrades:0, quorum echoed 999
confirmed.correction:
Four corrections — the mechanism is right, the severity story is partly wrong and it understates the worst case.

1. THE ON-SCREEN CLAIM IS OVERSTATED — the over-size quorum is NOT reachable through the interface. /home/user/CLAUDE-PROJECTS/ultimate-trading-system/public/construct.js:1084-1085 sends `const q = l.quorum ?? 1;` — the quorum comes from the leader row's own stored value, which lib/bracketwork.js:399-402 generates as `for (let k = 2; k <= memberCalls.length; k++)`, i.e. bounded by the committee size by construction. So quorum=999 requires a hand-typed URL; the owner cannot produce it from the screen.

2. AND THE RENDERED RESULT IS NOT "0 trades". committee.searchTrades/holdTrades appear on screen only inside the collapsed "the inspect record, verbatim" JSON block (construct.js:1126). The per-member column that IS rendered, "echoed by the vote", is `pctOf(m.withTradeHold)` where `pctOf = (v) => (v == null ? '—' : ...)` (construct.js:1109) — at an over-size quorum every row shows an em dash, not "0%". So the described misreading ("the committee never agreed") is not what the panel would actually print even if the URL were forged. Rank this as a silently-accepted impossible input on an API, not as a wrong number on the owner's screen.

3. THE ADVERSARY WALKED PAST THE WORSE, FULLY UI-REACHABLE BUG SITTING IN ITS OWN OBSERVATION. It noted "quorum=4 -> withTradeHold:1 for every member off just 2 hold trades" and treated that as background. It is the actual defect. `withTradeRate` (lib/inspect.js:26-36) counts only periods where the committee call is non-zero; at quorum == committee size a non-zero call requires all n members to have voted the same direction, so every member's vote matches the trade BY DEFINITION. withTradeHold is 100% for every member at unanimity, always, on any data. That value is rendered on screen as "echoed by the vote: 100.0%" — a real-looking percentage — and quorum == committee size (6 of 6, 8 of 8) is exactly what the sweep produces and what construct.js sends. Worse, there is no minimum-denominator floor: my run produced 100.0% for all four members off 2 hold trades, while the neighbouring `pairAgreement` deliberately returns null below `minOverlap = 5`. The column's own tooltip sells it as evidence of independence ("a member echoed by the others adds agreement without adding an independent opinion") — at unanimity it is a tautology reported as a measurement, with the denominator not shown next to it. That is the plausible-wrong-answer failure this project cares about, and it needs no forged URL.

4. TWO SILENT ACCEPTANCES THE REPORT MISSED. (a) Non-integer quorum is accepted and effectively ceils while echoing the fraction: quorum=1.5 -> echoed 1.5, holdTrades 3 (same as q2); quorum=3.9 -> echoed 3.9, holdTrades 2 (same as q4); quorum=4.0000001 -> echoed 4.0000001, holdTrades 0 — so a 4-member committee flips from "2 trades" to "0 trades" on a 1e-7 change in a number that can only meaningfully be a whole count. Also quorum='0x4' and ' 4 ' are accepted as 4, while '4abc' silently becomes 1. (b) quorum=Infinity is worse than 1e308: `Math.max(1, Infinity)` is Infinity, which JSON.stringify emits as null, so the response is `"quorum": null` with 0 trades — the endpoint does not even echo the impossible input back, it reports a null agreement level. Observed: HTTP 200, quorum echoed null, committee {"searchTrades":0,"holdTrades":0,...}.

The stated fix (400 on a quorum above the committee size) is right and matches lib/batch.js:387-393, but it should also reject non-integers and non-finite values, and — separately — lib/batch.js:401-403 (`raw.quorum`) has the same missing upper bound: `if (!Number.isInteger(q) || q < 1) throw ...` with no cap against the committee size, unlike the quorumSingles/quorumContexts branch three lines above it.

confirmed.title: keyRef set to whitespace reports 'set' on every screen but the live gate treats it as missing
confirmed.attack: POST /api/live/setups/:id/config {"keyRef":"   "}. validateOperational only checks `typeof keyRef === 'string'` (whitespace passes). summarize() reports keyRef as `s.keyRef ? 'set' : null` — a whitespace string is truthy, so it shows 'set'. But liveGateErrors / channels use `s.keyRef.trim()`, so going live is refused for a missing sub-account key.
confirmed.observed: After {"keyRef":"   "}: GET /api/live/setups list -> keyRef:'set'; GET /api/live/setups/:id detail -> keyRef:'set'; on-disk value is '   '. Transition to live -> 400 '... a LIVE setup needs its own sub-account keyRef ...'. configs list keyRefSet is computed with trim() (false), so that one field disagrees with the summarize 'set' on the same record.
confirmed.expected: One record must not report 'the sub-account key is set' on the setups screens while the go-live gate and the configs screen say it is unset — that is the RULE TWO / screen-vs-enforcement disagreement the project treats as a defect. keyRef should be trimmed on write (empty/whitespace -> null) so presence means the same thing everywhere.
confirmed.reproduce:
curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"keyRef":"   "}' http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/live/setups/<id>/config
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8531/api/live/setups | grep keyRef   # -> 'set', but go-live is refused
confirmed.correction:
The finding stands as described; two corrections to scope/severity, one of which makes the underlying defect considerably worse than reported.

(a) SEVERITY DOWN on the whitespace path itself: it is API-only and cannot reach real money. public/trade.html:626 already trims — `const keyRef=$('#keyIn').value.trim();` then posts `{keyRef: keyRef||null}` — so a person typing spaces into the field labelled "Sub-account key" and pressing "Save routing" stores null, not whitespace. I also confirmed the gate cannot be walked around from a trading state:
  live + {"keyRef":"   "} -> {"error":"update would break live execution: a LIVE setup needs its own sub-account keyRef..."}
So the harm of the reported attack is exactly the screen-vs-enforcement disagreement, not a mis-routed real order. Trimming keyRef on write is still the right fix, but it is a display-integrity fix, not a money fix.

(b) SEVERITY UP on the ROOT CAUSE, via a variant that IS reachable from the screen and IS silent. The detail endpoint returns the presence token in the same field name as the value (`keyRef: 'set'`), and public/trade.html:589 prefills the editor from that same field: `<input id="keyIn" value="${esc(s.keyRef||'')}" ...>`.   3) POST {"keyRef":"set","executionTargetRef":null}  (exactly what saveRouting sends) -> {"ok":true,...}

The real sub-account reference is destroyed and replaced by the string "set"; nothing anywhere complains, because "set" is a non-empty trimmed string that satisfies liveGateErrors, and every screen keeps saying the key is set. One factual error in the OBSERVED section, and it points at a slightly worse case than the one reported.

WRONG: "Objects/arrays are correctly refused by the charset regex." Objects are refused ({} -> HTTP 400). ARRAYS ARE NOT. `String(["Ghost-Cycle"])` is `"Ghost-Cycle"`, which sails through the charset regex:

  # campaign genuinely set first
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Aug-Cycle-3"}' http://127.0.0.1:8577/api/campaign
  -> {"name":"Aug-Cycle-3"}
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":[]}' http://127.0.0.1:8577/api/campaign
  -> HTTP 200 {"name":""}          <-- live campaign SILENTLY WIPED
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8577/api/campaign
  -> {"name":""}
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":["Ghost-Cycle"]}' http://127.0.0.1:8577/api/campaign
  -> HTTP 200 {"name":"Ghost-Cycle"}   <-- array SET the campaign

Arrays are refused only by accident, and only some of them: ["a","b"] -> HTTP 400 solely because String() joins with a comma and the comma is not in the charset. Any single-element array of a legal name is accepted, and an empty array is accepted as a clear. The validator has no type gate at all — `String(raw ?? '')` is the only thing standing between the caller and the stored value, and it happily flattens arrays.

The `[]` case is the one worth ranking above the report's "Minor". Under this project's own doctrine — an input silently ACCEPTED that should have been refused ranks above a 500 — a wrong-typed body that returns HTTP 200 while destroying the owner's current campaign is a different class from a boolean being relabelled "true". A caller sending the wrong shape gets a success response, and every run launched afterwards is stamped campaign:null with nothing anywhere saying the setting was dropped.

It stays bounded, and the report is right about why: campaign is a pure label (lib/compare.js:99-100 NEVER_ATTRIBUTABLE, "pure labels ... never shape money"), the wipe is visible on the next read of the campaign, and nothing in public/construct.js can produce an array from a DOM input value. So: correct finding, correct severity for the boolean/number case, but the arrays-are-safe parenthetical is false and hides the more interesting variant.

Two smaller notes: `{"name":{"toString":"x"}}` returns HTTP 400 {"error":"Cannot convert object to primitive value"} — the TypeError from String() is caught by the route's try/catch, so it is a 400 with a leaked internal message rather than a 500. And `{"name":".."}` is accepted (HTTP 200), harmless here only because the campaign name is never used as a path component.

  transition('negdraft','live')           -> REFUSED: NOT_LIVE_EXECUTABLE - cannot go live: cell.entry 'undefined' ...
And atomicWrite writes to `${file}.tmp${pid}` before rename, and that tmp name does not end in .json, so listSetups cannot pick up a half-written file. A hostile or malformed record therefore requires write access to data/live/setups/ — hand-edit, restore, partial rsync, cross-version schema change. Still exactly the project's own doctrine (a record that reads back plausibly wrong), but it is not a remote input surface.

WRONG — "any unrecognised state is treated as REAL money" is true of the SCREEN only, not of execution. I ran it:

  -> live REFUSED: BAD_TRANSITION - illegal transition ARMED -> live (allowed: none)   [same for stopped/retired/paper]
The rogue-state record is inert-but-mislabelled, not armed with real money. Say "displayed as a real book" and the finding survives intact; "REAL money" overstates it and is the one line a reviewer can knock down.

UNDERSOLD #1 — the duplicate-id collapse is the sharpest thing here and the report only lists it. Two files both carrying id "dup" give TWO rows over HTTP (dup A: LTCUSDT clip 10; dup B: XRPUSDT clip 99999) but ONE allowlist key, and the last one wins:

So the box enforces XRPUSDT at clip 99999 while the owner is simultaneously looking at a row that says LTCUSDT at clip 10. Which one wins is decided by listSetups' sort on createdUtc — a field in the file. That is a plausible wrong answer with money attached, ranked above the tHours case.

UNDERSOLD #2 — id != filename splits the list from every other endpoint. getSetup resolves by FILENAME, listSetups reports the in-file id. Every row in my list 404s on detail:

  GET /api/live/setups/dup / str-thours / negclip -> 404 likewise

UNDERSOLD #3 — the 2 dropped files are the same defect pointed the other way, not a footnote. .filter(Boolean) after a swallowed catch means a LIVE setup whose file becomes unreadable simply vanishes from listSetups, therefore vanishes from the allowlist on the next carry, and the box stops honouring it while its real position is still open. FACTUAL — the report says "four rows that are just {keyRef:null}" and blames "the scalars and the empty object", and implies 20000-deep nesting was one of the two drops. Neither holds. I checked each file individually:

The defect is real and the mechanism is described correctly, but three things in the write-up need fixing — one wording error, one missing severity qualifier, and one under-stated root cause.

1. "COMPLETELY INVISIBLE" IS WRONG — AND THE TRUTH IS WORSE. The duplicate does show. /api/live/setups returns both records, and drawSetups() in public/trade.html filters with `rows=(d.setups||[]).filter(s=>wanted.has(s.id))` — a duplicate id passes twice, so both rows draw. After the stop, one row reads stopped and the other still reads live. What is broken is not visibility but CONTROLLABILITY: both rows carry `data-id="${s.id}"`, i.e. "twin" for both, so clicking either opens the same record, and every control resolves `${id}.json`. Observed over HTTP against the row still showing live:
     POST .../twin/state {"to":"stopped"} -> {"error":"illegal transition stopped -> stopped (allowed: paper, live, retired)"}
     DELETE /api/live/setups/twin        -> {"error":"only drafts may be deleted; use retire"}
   Retiring the reachable copy took twin.json to retired and left the duplicate live. So the owner is left looking at a live row that no route can stop. Reword the finding as "visible but unreachable", and lead with the genuinely silent half — the FIRST stop returning {"ok":true,...,"state":"stopped"} while the box keeps a live 250000 entry.

2. MISSING SEVERITY QUALIFIER: THIS IS NOT REMOTELY REACHABLE. No route and no shipped script can produce it. createSetup refuses when `${id}.json` already exists, and the only non-test writer of a setup file in the tree is atomicWrite(fileFor(id)) in lib/live/setups.js, always `${id}.json`. deploy/install.sh:106 states greenlights, setups, journals and book state are deliberately not copied. The crash-safe tmp file is `${file}.tmp${pid}`, which fails the `.endsWith('.json')` filter and is ignored. So it takes a direct filesystem write into data/live/setups/ — a hand copy, a restore, an editor backup. That is a genuine hazard for a no-database file-per-record system where the owner handles the files, but it should be ranked as an operator/backup hazard, not an accepted input.

3. ROOT CAUSE IS BROADER THAN DUPLICATE IDS, AND THE SINGLE-FILE CASE IS WORSE. The registry never checks that the id inside a file matches its filename; duplicates are one symptom. One file `archived-2026-08-01.json` containing "id":"ghost", state live, clipUsd 99000:
     listSetups() -> 1 row: id="ghost" state=live clipUsd=99000
     allowlistFrom -> {"ghost":{...,"max_clip_usd":99000,"state":"live","key_ref":"kG"}}
     getSetup("ghost") -> null
     transition/updateSetup/deleteDraft/setRunEpoch -> all THREW NOT_FOUND: no such setup ghost
     state on disk after every attempt: live
   A record the box will trade at 99k that no control can touch at all. So the EXPECTED should be stated as "the filename must equal the record's id, and the registry must refuse to serve any file where it does not" — that covers both the duplicate and the lone mis-named file, whereas a duplicate-only check misses the worse case.

4. MINOR, on ordering: "the LAST one wins by readdir/createdUtc order" is right, worth making precise. listSetups sorts by createdUtc localeCompare and allowlistFrom's last write wins, so the latest createdUtc wins; on ties it falls to readdir order. A byte-identical `cp` ties on createdUtc, so which record reaches the box is then decided by filename ordering. Nothing does the flagging: the field is write-only. A record written by a future (or a foreign) schema is parsed with today's assumptions and its unknown fields are carried along untouched — including through updateSetup, which spreads the whole record and writes it back. Either the readers gate on the version or the field should not be there claiming a protection that does not exist.

confirmed.correction:
The observations are real; the finding points at the wrong field, proposes a remedy that does not close the hole, mischaracterizes updateSetup, and overstates severity.

1) THE PROPOSED REMEDY IS TRIVIALLY BYPASSED. The version is data in the same attacker-controlled file. I took the identical poisoned record, flipped `"schema": 99` back to `"schema": 1` and engineVersion to `gc-1.0.0/setup-1/config-1`, and re-read it: `schema: 1 | unknownFutureField still there: "MEANING CHANGED IN v99"`. Any conceivable version gate passes this. A gate stops an *honest* future writer — but the only code that writes setups is lib/live/greenlight.js:250 calling createSetup, which always stamps the current constant at line 91. The honest writer can never produce a mismatched version, so the gate would be dead code guarding a case the codebase cannot generate.

2) THE REAL GAP IS ELSEWHERE AND IS BIGGER: there is NO read-time validation at all. getSetup (setups.js:133) and listSetups (setups.js:140) are bare JSON.parse. validateOperational (line 59) exists and runs only on create and update. I demonstrated this with a record declaring the CURRENT schema 1 and `clipUsd: -999999`, `stopPct: 0.00001` — both rejected by validateOperational at create. GET /api/live/setups served it as `{"id":"current-schema-junk","name":"looks completely normal","state":"live","clipUsd":-999999,"stopPct":1e-05,...}`, and /status returned those same values beside a live-looking `nextEntryUtc":"2026-08-22T00:00:0...`. That is exactly the project's "plausible wrong answer" shape — and a schema gate catches none of it, because the record honestly declares version 1.

3) updateSetup IS A GUARD, NOT A HOLE. The report casts it as a silent carry-along door. It does spread unknown fields (`next = {...s}`, line 199 — true), but it re-runs validateOperational on the merged record at line 201 and is in fact the one place that catches a poisoned record. My edit attempt was refused: `BAD_SETUP - clipUsd: must be a positive dollar notional; stopPct: below the 0.005 floor (0.5%) — triggers on noise`. Separately, the carried unknown fields are inert: grep found no generic iteration over a setup record (no `Object.keys(s)`, `Object.entries(s)`, or `for...in`), so nothing reads `unknownFutureField` — it is dead weight in the JSON, not a behavior change.

4) SEVERITY IS OVERSTATED BECAUSE OF THE ENTRY VECTOR. routes.js's header states "Deliberately ABSENT: a create endpoint"; the sole writer is the greenlight shuttle. Every attack here required writing the JSON file directly. Anyone with filesystem write access to data/live/setups/ can already set state:"live", clipUsd and keyRef to anything, so the version field grants them nothing extra. This is not an "input silently accepted" defect in the sense the doctrine ranks highest — it is a missing defense-in-depth integrity check against file corruption, hand-editing, a partial write, or a restore from a bad backup.

WHAT SURVIVES, as a modest but fair finding: version.js's comment claims the version lets a later upgrade "flag the setup for re-validation instead of silently changing what its config means", and nothing does that — the comment advertises a protection that does not exist. Notably the project already version-gates elsewhere (lib/compare.js:124 emits "ENGINE VERSIONS DIFFER ... read deltas with suspicion"; lib/planted.js:363 gates on `verdict.engineVersion === currentVersion`), so the precedent exists in the experiment path but not the live-money path. The correct remedy is the report's second option, not its first: either delete the misleading comment, or — better and independent of the version — validate on read so getSetup/listSetups refuse or loudly mark a record that validateOperational would not have created.

confirmed.correction:
The finding stands, but the named cause - and therefore the proposed fix - is wrong.

1) validatePolicy is not what accepted this. POST /api/live/setups/:id/config (lib/live/routes.js:155) calls reg.updateSetup, which validates with validateOperational (lib/live/setups.js:59-74). That function inspects id, ownerId, name, state, clipUsd, stopPct and three string refs - it never looks at trainPolicy. trainPolicy is simply in MUTABLE (lib/live/setups.js:148) and written through verbatim. This route applies ZERO validation to trainPolicy, so the hole is far wider than a missing upper bound. All of these returned HTTP 200 and were stored exactly as sent:

  {"trainPolicy":{"mode":"whenever","throughMs":1700000000000}} -> stored {'mode':'whenever','throughMs':1700000000000}
  {"trainPolicy":"banana"}                                     -> stored 'banana'
  {"trainPolicy":{"mode":"frozen"}}                            -> stored {'mode':'frozen'}  (no throughMs at all)
  {"trainPolicy":{"mode":"frozen","throughMs":-5}}             -> stored {'mode':'frozen','throughMs':-5}
  {"trainPolicy":{"mode":"rolling","throughMs":1700000000000}} -> stored {'mode':'rolling','throughMs':1700000000000}

Every one of those is a shape validatePolicy already rejects. They get in because validatePolicy is never consulted on this route.

2) Bounding throughMs inside validatePolicy would fix nothing here. validatePolicy has exactly one non-test caller, channels.activate (lib/live/channels.js:66), guarded by `if (trainPolicy)`. The only HTTP door into activate is POST /api/live/configs/:id/activate (lib/live/routes.js:284-292), which forwards only channel, clipUsd and name - never trainPolicy. So validatePolicy is currently reachable from no HTTP route at all, and POST /api/live/setups/:id/config is the only way a trainPolicy is ever set from outside. The fix needs two parts: (a) run validatePolicy on any trainPolicy patch in updateSetup, so both doors agree; and (b) bound a frozen throughMs at or before now inside validatePolicy.

  cacheState -> {"symbol":"DEADUSDT","months":1,"from":"2024-03","to":"2024-03","toMonth":"2024-03"}
`Array.isArray([])` is true, so that file is a cache HIT forever. The month is never revisited, contributes zero candles, and is counted as a full month by every coverage number the owner can see. That is the plausible-wrong-answer shape this project cares about, and it needs no adversary at all.

A SECOND DEFECT THE REPORT WALKED PAST. lib/pipeline.js:105-110 documents "all loaded data" mode as "never touches the network ... monthlyKlines is only called for months whose bundle file exists on disk, so it always cache-hits and the no-network guarantee holds." That is false whenever a bundle on disk is unparseable or not an array. Three of the four scenarios broke the guarantee in the adversary's own runs; the fetch was there to be seen and was not looked for.

SEVERITY, corrected: rank `[]` high — silent, permanent, self-inflicted, undercounted by every visible number. Rank truncated / 0-byte / object-not-array low as data loss (they self-repair or throw), but note them as a stated-guarantee breach instead.

MINOR: the absent-file case is overstated. cacheState reported months:5 next to from 2024-01 / to 2024-06, and server.js:96 passes the whole row through, so the count is not hidden — only from/to imply contiguity. (I have not read the code that renders those values, so I am not naming what the screen calls them.)

The EXPECTED section is right in substance, and the second half is the better half: reading months is derived from filenames and every number the run produces is derived from contents, and nothing compares them. `[]` is the case that proves it, because there refusing is not even available — the file parses fine, it is simply empty, and only a read-count-vs-name-count comparison catches it.

confirmed.title: A month file holding another month's candles reports 720 candles that do not exist — the count the owner reads is higher than the number of distinct hours loaded
confirmed.attack: Wrote April's 720 candles into FAKEAUSDT-1h-2024-03.json while the real April bundle was also present, then loaded both the ranged and all-loaded paths.
confirmed.expected: monthlyKlines should verify that a cached month's rows fall inside the month its filename names, and reject the file if they do not. Failing that, the count reported to the owner should be distinct hours, not raw rows — a candle count that double-counts is worse than no count.

confirmed.correction:
The finding stands, but it is scoped too narrowly in three ways — the miscount is the least of what I observed.

1) THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION IS MISSING FROM THE REPORT. In the case tested (March's filename holding April's rows) the real April bundle is read LATER, so its rows win the Map and prices are unharmed — only March vanishes. Reverse the direction and the wrong rows land last and silently OVERWRITE real prices. I wrote April's 720 rows into FAKEAUSDT-1h-2024-05.json:
HONEST  April 01 00:00 close= 104  April 15 12:00 close= 107.48  rows= 4368  hours= 4368
SPOOF   April 01 00:00 close= 999  April 15 12:00 close= 1002.48  rows= 4344  hours= 3624
SPOOF   per-month distinct hours {"2024-01":744,"2024-02":696,"2024-03":744,"2024-04":720,"2024-06":720}
SPOOF   ranged candles reported = 4344  monthsWithoutBundles= []
That is not a miscount, it is wrong prices with the right units and a believable magnitude feeding buildChunks and everything trained on it — the exact failure class this project ranks highest — and the reported count and the coverage feed both stay clean.

2) THE HOLE IS NOT ONLY IN monthlyKlines. monthFromDayFiles (lib/binance.js:293) accepts out-of-day rows identically. Day files for FAKEBUSDT 2024-03-01..05 with the 03-03 file holding the 4th's candles:
DAYFILES honest  rows= 120  distinctHours= 120
DAYFILES spoiled rows= 120  distinctHours= 96  2024-03-04T00 close= 104  2024-03-03T00 present? false
cacheState: [{"symbol":"FAKEBUSDT","months":1,"from":"2024-03","to":"2024-03-05","toMonth":"2024-03"}]
A fix scoped to monthlyKlines alone leaves the day-file tier open, and loadSymbol feeds day-file rows into the same `candles` number.

3) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM CATCHES IT. The 31 dropped chunks the report saw never reach anyone: buildChunks returns `dropped` (lib/dataset.js:188-238) and its callers in lib/bracket.js:59-68 destructure only `.chunks`; no consumer of that counter exists in server.js or public/construct.js. Losing ~31 of ~150 chunks does not trip MIN_CHUNKS=12 either.

Two honest qualifications the report should carry:
- Reachability: no in-app write path can produce such a file. planted.js buckets every row by its own ts before writing (lib/planted.js:167-172), and monthlyKlines writes back exactly what the named Binance zip parsed to. This requires the file on disk to already be wrong — tampering, a hand-restored cache directory, or a mislabeled upstream zip. In-scope for a stored-data attack, but it is not triggerable through the interface.
- The expectation's fallback is too weak. Reporting distinct hours instead of raw rows fixes the number and nothing else: March would still be silently absent while /api/data-state claims six months, and in case (1) the prices would still be wrong with a perfectly correct hour count. The real requirement is a read-side check that a cached file's rows fall inside the period its filename names — in monthlyKlines AND monthFromDayFiles — with the failure surfaced, not a corrected tally.

confirmed.title: Timestamps not on the hour load in full and are counted in full, but are invisible to the chunker — 4368 candles produce 149 chunks instead of 181
confirmed.attack: Shifted every 2024-03 timestamp by +30 minutes (ts + 1800000) in the cache file and ran the full read -> fill -> chunk path.
confirmed.expected: The cache-read path should apply the same hour alignment the download path does, or reject a month whose timestamps are not on the bucket boundary. A row set that is 100% present and 0% usable is the exact shape of a plausible wrong answer: the coverage says full, the score is computed on 82% of the range.
confirmed.reproduce: cd /tmp/claude-0/.../scratchpad/sbx && node drive1.js   # scenario 'timestamps off the hour (+30 min) for all march'
confirmed.correction:
The finding stands. Four corrections to the framing, two of which make it WORSE than described and two of which calibrate it.

WORSE #1 — the one internal signal that would expose this is thrown away before it can reach anything. buildChunks returns `dropped` and `considered`, but the only production caller destructures them off: lib/bracket.js:59 and :64 are `const { chunks } = buildChunks(...)`, and :67-68 are `buildChunks(...).chunks`. So `gap: 31` is computed and discarded inside the library. The only downstream check on chunk count is `if (chunks.length < MIN_CHUNKS)` at lib/bracketwork.js:135, with MIN_CHUNKS = 12 (lib/pipeline.js:21). 149 sails through with 12x margin. I grepped the whole tree: nothing outside lib/dataset.js and tests reads `dropped.gap`. (public/construct.js:1650 shows a "dropped" figure, but that is `v.folds.dropped` from lib/httwo.js:190 — walk-forward folds, unrelated.)

WORSE #2 — no coverage number CAN contradict the contents, by construction. cachedMonths (lib/binance.js:254-267), cachedDayMonths (:275-288), coveredMonths (:322-324) and cacheState (:328-368) all derive coverage from FILENAMES via regex on readdirSync — they never open a file. So "6 months, 2024-01 to 2024-06" is a statement about four filenames, not about 4368 candles, and it would read identically if every file contained garbage.

CALIBRATION #1 — "no missing months" is not a corroborating number, it is a vacuous one. loadSymbolAll hardcodes `return { rows, missing: [], cachedMonthCount: list.length }` (lib/pipeline.js:123). `missingA: []` comes back empty on every call down this path regardless of data state. Citing it as one of the reassuring numbers overstates the case slightly (though the underlying point — nothing contradicts you — holds).

CALIBRATION #2 — the magnitude is geometry-dependent, not a fixed 82%. I re-ran the identical mutation under weekly-8d: CONTROL {"chunks":25,"dropped":{"gap":0,"noLabel":0},"considered":26,"up":3,"down":4,"flat":18} vs MARCH+30m {"chunks":20,"dropped":{"gap":5,"noLabel":0},"considered":26,"up":3,"down":4,"flat":13}. So 149/181 = 82% for daily-1d, 20/25 = 80% for weekly-8d. One month of 6 corrupted costs roughly one month of samples in either shape — reasonable, but "82%" is the daily-1d number, not a property of the defect.

ON REALISM — the trigger is external, but "external" includes the project's own installer, which is more than tampering. I checked every writer into data/cache and all of them align: parseKlineCsv floors (lib/binance.js:95), recentKlines floors (`Math.floor(Number(r[0]) / HOUR_MS) * HOUR_MS`, :242), dailyKlines routes through parseKlineCsv with HOUR_MS (:170), and lib/planted.js:168 constructs `ts = t0 + (d * 24 + h) * HOUR_MS` from a UTC month start. There is no route in server.js that accepts candle JSON (the only cache-touching routes are /api/data/download, /api/data/refresh, /api/data/purge at server.js:130/174/227, and purge only unlinks). BUT deploy/install.sh:108-124 rsyncs a DIFFERENT project's candle cache — `/opt/general-classifier/data/cache` — wholesale into this system's data/cache on first install, with checks for free disk space and nothing whatsoever for file format, row shape, or timestamp bucketing. That is a designed-in, documented path for foreign-format candle JSON to enter this unnormalised read path.

ON THE EXPECTATION — the first half of it ("apply the same hour alignment the download path does") is the wrong fix and would manufacture a second plausible wrong answer. (a) monthlyKlines is interval-parameterised and also serves 1m files at bucketMs 60_000 (lib/binance.js:124, :139); flooring on read to a hardcoded HOUR_MS would collapse 60 minute-candles onto one key and silently discard 59 of them — the exact failure the parseKlineCsv comment at :80-84 warns about. (b) Even with the right bucket, flooring on read silently MOVES every candle back by up to 59 minutes and silently collapses collisions, i.e. it invents an alignment the file never asserted. For a file whose contents disagree with the format this app writes, the only non-inventing option is the second half: refuse the month loudly, or at minimum surface the misalignment count. Recommend striking the "floor it" half.

ONE ESCALATION I TRIED THAT FAILED, reported honestly: I hypothesised that PARTIAL off-hour corruption would be worse — leaving one-hour holes that forwardFill would paper over with fabricated flat candles, keeping the chunk count intact while poisoning the prices. It does not happen. Shifting every 4th and every 2nd March row gave fillsA 0 and 0 fabricated candles, because forwardFill computes `gapHours = (times[i] - times[i-1]) / HOUR_MS - 1` and sub-hour spacing makes that negative, so the `if (gapHours <= 0 ...) continue` guard at lib/dataset.js:75 skips it. Results were {"chunks":150,"dropped":{"gap":31,"noLabel":1}} and {"chunks":149,"dropped":{"gap":31,"noLabel":2}} — the same 31 gap drops, not worse. The defect drops data; it does not fabricate it.

confirmed.title: Duplicate timestamps: which of two conflicting prices becomes the truth is decided by the order they happen to sit in the file
confirmed.attack: Duplicated every 2024-03 candle, with the duplicate priced +20. Ran it twice — once with the good copy first, once with the corrupt copy first — and read the entry price and label of the chunk starting 2024-03-12.
confirmed.expected: A repeated timestamp with a DIFFERENT price is a corrupt file and should be refused. A repeated timestamp with the same price could be deduped silently, but the two cases must be told apart rather than both resolved by array position.
confirmed.reproduce: cd /tmp/claude-0/.../scratchpad/sbx && node drive4.js   # section F
confirmed.correction:
The defect is real and I would rank it HIGHER than the report does, but three parts of the write-up need fixing.

1) THE DETERMINISM CLAUSE IS WRONG — drop it. "The project's own determinism guarantee holds only because file order happens to be stable — nothing checks it" is not what I measured. The guarantee (lib/bracketwork.js:12-14, "Two runs of the same descriptor produce byte-identical numbers") is NOT violated. Three consecutive runs over the same duplicated file:
    same dup file, 3 runs   123.014883 123.014883 123.014883   identical: true
   JSON array order is stable across parses, and the app's own parser preserves equal-ts order too — `rows.sort((a,b)=>a.ts-b.ts)` at lib/binance.js:107 is a stable sort. I fed parseKlineCsv two rows with identical openTime 1710201600000, opens 999 then 111:
    parseKlineCsv equal-ts   [999,111]
   So row order is a STABLE input, not a lottery. The correct statement is not "non-deterministic" but "the answer is selected by a property of the file that carries no meaning": two files holding the same SET of candles produce different prices, different P&L and different labels. That is a soundness/reproducibility defect, not a determinism-guarantee breach — and claiming the latter is the kind of overreach that gets a real finding dismissed.

2) THE SEVERITY IS UNDERSTATED. The report's own example moved diffPct but left the label at 0, which reads as cosmetic. It is not. I duplicated exactly ONE row — the entry candle at 2024-03-12 + 25h — priced +8, and the label flips:
    clean                    {"rows":4368,"map":4368,"chunks":181,"entry":103.014883,"exit":101.627491,"diffPct":-1.3467879199552082,"label":0,"up":65,"down":63,"flat":53}
    ONE dup row (good,bad)   {"rows":4369,"map":4368,"chunks":181,"entry":111.014883,"exit":101.627491,"diffPct":-8.455976123489668,"label":-1,"up":65,"down":64,"flat":52}
    ONE dup row (bad,good)   {"rows":4369,"map":4368,"chunks":181,"entry":103.014883,"exit":101.627491,"diffPct":-1.3467879199552082,"label":0,"up":65,"down":63,"flat":53}
   One extra row out of 4,369 — a 4369-vs-4368 discrepancy nothing reports — moves that chunk's move from -1.35% to -8.46%, flips its training label from flat to down, and shifts the whole run's label mix (flat 53->52, down 63->64). It is exactly the doctrine's dangerous case: right units, believable magnitude, wrong number.

3) THE "REPORTED CANDLE COUNT" CLAIM IS RIGHT BUT UNSOURCED — here is the path. `loadSymbol`'s rows.length is returned as `candles` by /api/data/download (server.js:155) and /api/data/refresh (server.js:210), and public/construct.js:370 renders it as `${sym}: ${r.candles || 0} candles`. I ran loadSymbol over the duplicated month:
    loadSymbol 2024-03 rows   1488   (March has 744 real hours)
   So the doubled count does reach the owner's screen as a "…candles" line, while the map the sweep actually trains on holds 744.

4) THE EXPECTATION IS RIGHT BUT TOO NARROW. "Refuse a repeated timestamp with a different price" fixes one symptom of a wider hole: the cache-read path validates nothing. parseKlineCsv rejects non-positive OHLC (lib/binance.js:97), but that guard only ever runs on a fresh download — a cached file is trusted wholesale at lib/binance.js:126-129. A cache file with a negative open on the entry candle sailed through:
    negative entry open      {"entry":-5,"diffPct":-2132.54982,"label":-1}
   The check belongs at the cache read, one place, covering strictly-increasing ts AND positive OHLC — not just the duplicate case.

5) REACHABILITY — an honest partial mitigation the report omits. I could not find an app-internal path that manufactures a duplicate timestamp. Binance monthly 1h zips have unique open times and parseKlineCsv sorts them; both read paths prefer the monthly bundle over day files (`monthly.has(mm) ? monthlyKlines(...) : monthFromDayFiles(...)`, lib/pipeline.js:116-118, and the same precedence in loadSymbol), so the two storage forms never concatenate for one month; lib/planted.js:168 generates strictly increasing ts. The corrupt file therefore has to arrive from outside — hand edit, partial restore, backup/rsync mishap, anomalous upstream zip. That lowers likelihood, not severity: lib/binance.js:122-123 states "Past months never change, so a parsed month is cached on disk and reused forever", so once such a file lands it is silently authoritative from then on.

6) ONE AGGRAVATING FACT THE REPORT MISSED. This exact hazard is already documented in the codebase and was fixed in only one caller. parseKlineCsv's header (lib/binance.js:69-73) says the hourly bucket is "catastrophic" for 1m files because "all sixty minutes of an hour would land on the same key and fifty-nine of them would be discarded by the Map that consumes them — silently, with no error and a plausible result." The mitigation chosen was caller discipline (pass bucketMs=60_000), not a guard at the Map. So last-writer-wins in toHourlyMap is a known failure mode that was patched at one call site and left open at the one that feeds every sweep.

confirmed.title: Month numbers 00 and 13 are accepted from disk and served by /api/data-state as the data range — the typed input is validated, the on-disk input is not
confirmed.attack: Placed FAKEAUSDT-1h-2024-00.json and FAKEAUSDT-1h-2024-13.json beside six real months, started the sandbox server on port 8567 and called GET /api/data-state.
confirmed.expected: The same month validation on both sides of the boundary. A filename naming month 00 or 13 should be ignored (or surfaced as junk), and the span the coverage row reports should be derived from data actually read, not from filenames.
confirmed.reproduce:
cd /tmp/claude-0/.../scratchpad/sbx && node drive4.js   # section H
# then: PORT=8567 node /tmp/.../scratchpad/sbx/server.js & curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8567/api/data-state
confirmed.correction:
Three corrections. Two raise severity, one moves it.

1. "The typed input is validated" is FALSE for the destructive route. It holds only for download/refresh (which go through monthList). /api/data/purge — the "trim…" button — checks shape `^\d{4}-\d{2}$` and nothing else, then compares months as strings. All three of these were ACCEPTED, HTTP 200, no complaint:
  {"symbol":"FAKEAUSDT","keepFrom":"2024-13","keepTo":"2024-13"} -> {"purged":7,...} — six real months plus 2024-00 deleted, only the impossible month left standing; /api/data-state then read months=1, from=2024-13, to=2024-13.
  {"symbol":"FAKEBUSDT","keepFrom":"2024-99","keepTo":"2024-99"} -> {"purged":7,...} — every month gone. A "keep this range" instruction that deletes everything.
  {"symbol":"FAKEBUSDT","keepFrom":"2024-06","keepTo":"2024-01"} -> {"purged":7,...} — both months perfectly valid, merely inverted; monthList would have thrown 'end month is before start month', purge does not use monthList. Every file deleted.
public/construct.js:385-389 feeds these from two free-text prompt() calls, not a month picker, so a typo goes straight through. By this project's own ranking — an input silently accepted outranks a 500 — this typed, accepted, irreversible one outranks the read-side finding the report leads with.

2. The impossible-month half is BOTH overstated and understated.
  Overstated as a live state: nothing in the system can write a -2024-00.json or -2024-13.json. cachePath is reached only from loadSymbol (months from monthList, validated) and loadSymbolAll (which only re-derives names already on disk). Those two files exist because the attacker placed them. It is a genuine trust-boundary hole, not something the running system produces.
  Understated as a consequence: the damage is worse than 1488 candles. lib/planted.js plantedSpan() consumes cacheState()'s from/to. With the two files present I measured
    plantedSpan() -> {"fromMonth":"2024-00","toDate":"2024-13-31"}  -> t0 2023-12-01, end 2025-01-31, days = 428
  and with the stray 2019-07 also present
    plantedSpan() -> {"fromMonth":"2019-07","toDate":"2024-13-31"}  -> days = 2042
  against ~186 days of real candles per pair. generateFabricated takes that span and WRITES the fabricated pair over it. So the planted-check subject — the instrument the whole gate rests on — gets regenerated over a span the real data does not have. That is the plausible-wrong-answer, more than the candle count is.
  One path is clean: refresh does not swallow it. POST /api/data/refresh {"symbol":"FAKEAUSDT"} returned job status "error", "bad month \"2024-13\"" — loud, correct, no silent carry.

3. The FAKEBUSDT half is misattributed, and is the more reachable defect of the two. It is not caused by a filename being junk. cacheState reports `from` = earliest cached month, `to` = latest, and never checks CONTIGUITY. Two ordinary legitimate downloads — 2019-07, later 2024-01..2024-06 — produce that identical row with no tampering whatsoever. The purge route also swallows unlink failures (`catch { /* reported below via recount */ }` at server.js:248), a second no-tampering route to a gappy span. So the EXPECTED clause should not be "ignore junk filenames" for this half; it should be that the coverage row has to show the span is not contiguous — months=7 spanning 60 calendar months is the misreading, and it needs no planted file to happen.
  Minor: the reporter's "7 months is really five months of candles" did not reproduce — with one `[]` bundle I got 7 reported against 6 candle-bearing months. The mechanism (an empty bundle counted as covered) is real; their count was specific to their fixture.

confirmed.title: A stray out-of-range month file makes the chunker consider 1,827 starts and drop 1,645 of them — and the count is discarded, so the run reports the same 181 chunks either way
confirmed.attack: Added FAKEAUSDT-1h-2019-07.json beside a clean 2024-01..2024-06 cache, then ran the all-loaded path.
confirmed.expected: `dropped.gap` and `considered` belong in the run record — they are the difference between "181 chunks from 182 candidate weeks" and "181 chunks from 1,827". A 90% drop rate is the single most informative number about whether a result should be believed, and it is computed and thrown away.
confirmed.reproduce: cd /tmp/claude-0/.../scratchpad/sbx && node drive1.js   # last scenario; and node drive3.js section E
confirmed.correction:
Four corrections. The mechanism is real; the story told about it is not.

1) "A run over 90% empty history" is not what happens. The two chunk sets are BIT-IDENTICAL — same startTs list, same labels (verified above). Nothing is computed over empty history. The 1,645 "drops" are phantom day-starts in 2019-08..2023-12, where no candle exists at all; they are an artifact of minTs jumping back through dailyStarts(), not lost data. Reporting the two runs with the same 181 chunks is CORRECT. This is a missing diagnostic, not a plausible wrong answer, and by the project's own ranking it sits below any silently-accepted bad input.

2) "Reported identically" is false. The run doc carries `dataManifest` (lib/batch.js:1427, lib/manifest.js), which sha256s every `<SYMBOL>-1h-*.json` in the cache. Real stampManifest output from my sandbox:
CLEAN   overallDigest=c4a8364efa0b87dd186c93b4 files(total)=12 {"FAKEAUSDT":{"files":6,"bytes":617535,...}}
STRAY19 overallDigest=ae4868fef04b58e5d2add267 files(total)=13 {"FAKEAUSDT":{"files":7,"bytes":722704,...}}
public/construct.js:942 renders that as "Data fingerprint:" with the digest and "N coin(s), M file(s)" under the heading "What this run actually is". Separately, cacheState() reports months 6 -> 7 and from "2024-01" -> "2019-07", and public/construct.js:322-329 renders that in the panel headed "Data on server" with columns pair / months / from / to. The stray file is visible in two places already.

3) The EXPECTED is actively harmful as stated. `dropped.gap`/`considered` as computed are not a data-quality signal — they anti-correlate with harm. Measured, same script, daily-1d:
A clean                            chunks=181 considered=182  gapDropped=0    dropRate=0.0%  testPeriods=36 testStart=2024-05-25
B clean + stray 2019-07 file       chunks=181 considered=1827 gapDropped=1645 dropRate=90.0% testPeriods=36 testStart=2024-05-25
C real hole: 2024-03 deleted       chunks=149 considered=182  gapDropped=31   dropRate=17.0% testPeriods=30 testStart=2024-05-31
D real hole: 24h missing in march  chunks=178 considered=182  gapDropped=2    dropRate=1.1%  testPeriods=36 testStart=2024-05-25
The 90% case is the undamaged one; the case that actually lost a sixth of the data reads 17%. Putting the raw counter in the run record would flag a perfect run as 90% bad and a genuinely degraded one as mildly off. To be the number the finding wants, it would have to count only starts that fall inside covered data.

4) The damaging cases are NOT invisible today. Row C shows chunks 181->149, testPeriods 36->30, and the recorded window start moving 2024-05-25 -> 2024-05-31. testPeriods is stored (lib/bracketwork.js:538 -> lib/batch.js:1459/1506/1582 as testPeriods/searchPeriods) along with windowStamps.testStartTs, and below MIN_CHUNKS=12 buildCombo throws "only N labelable chunks", which lands in doc.failures and renders as "N unit(s) FAILED".

Also: "the two load modes disagree by 744 candles with nothing naming the difference" is wrong. The difference IS the mode — 4368 is the six named months, 5112 is every cached month. It is chosen by the checkbox labelled "all loaded data" (public/construct.js:443), stored as params.allLoaded (lib/batch.js:1166), and listed in lib/verdict.js:92's WATCH array so a real-vs-null comparison names the mismatch out loud.

THE BETTER FINDING IS ONE LINE AWAY, and this attack walked past it. forwardFill returns a `fills` count of candles it INVENTED; its only production caller is lib/bracketwork.js:68 — `const filled = forwardFill(toHourlyMap(loaded.rows)).map;` — which discards it on the same line it takes the map. grep confirms no other production reader (lib/live/view.js's `fills` is order fills, unrelated). Deleting the single hour 2024-03-10 01:00 from an otherwise clean cache:
fills(honest)= 0  fills(1h outage)= 1  <-- BOTH DISCARDED by bracketwork getMap
chunks 181 181  considered 182 182  gapDropped 0 0
entry candle at 2024-03-10T01:00:00.000Z invented? true
honest  c1= 99.2968444085464  c2= 100.64662181267707 diffPct= 1.3593356487514807 label= 0
outage  c1= 99.22925938743887 c2= 100.64662181267707 diffPct= 1.4283714642111045 label= 0
chunks whose diffPct changed: 1 of 181
A fabricated candle became the entry price the outcome is measured from, the number moved, and every counter this finding wants surfaced (considered 182, gapDropped 0) stayed at its clean value. That is the plausible-wrong-answer version of the same "counter computed and thrown away" defect, and it is the one worth the owner's attention.

It reproduces, but three things in their write-up need fixing — two of them make it WORSE than reported, one makes part of it weaker.

1) THEY UNDERSTATED THE SEVERITY. They stopped at "unchanged coverage". The product has an explicit data-integrity report and it is blind to this by construction. lib/live/catalog.js:54 buildCatalog — its own header says it "turns 'did the user delete something?' into a MISSING/PRESENT list" — computes present/missing/ok purely from binance.coveredMonths(), which is filename-only. Measured (verify_catalog.js, 8 months of day files, 7 files truncated to half their bytes across 7 different months):
  CLEAN   rows= 5856  catalog.ok= true  missing= []  present= 8 months
  CORRUPT rows= 5688  catalog.ok= true  missing= []  present= 8 months
          hours lost = 168   catalog change = NONE
168 hours gone, catalog byte-identical and still ok:true. Worse, repair() (lib/live/catalog.js:83) only re-fetches months listed in e.missing — so the one mechanism built to rebuild lost candle data will never touch these files no matter how many times it is run. That is the real bite, not the coverage string.

2) THE COMMENT'S JUSTIFICATION IS EVEN THINNER THAN THEY SAID. They wrote "the comment justifies it as tolerating a concurrent write". Both writers of day files are already atomic tmp+rename: dailyKlines at lib/binance.js:183-185, and writeDayFiles at pilot-refresh.js:76-78. On POSIX a reader therefore sees either the whole old file or the whole new one — the torn read the comment names is essentially impossible. The catch cannot be doing the job it claims; the only thing it can actually absorb is permanent corruption, which is precisely what it must not absorb silently.

3) THEY OVERSTATED THE WRONG-MONTH ROW. Case D is real as I reproduced it, but it is NOT reachable through the app's own write paths. writeDayFiles (pilot-refresh.js:60-71) buckets each row by that row's own UTC year/month/day before choosing the filename, and dailyKlines names the file from the requested day and parses only that day's zip. So a July day file holding August candles needs a hand-placed or externally corrupted file. The truncated / empty / unparseable cases carry the weight — those have ordinary causes (crash mid-copy, full disk, a partial rsync of data/cache). Their EXPECTED asks for a filename-vs-content check; that is cheap belt-and-braces but it is not the fix that matters. The fix that matters is that an unreadable day file must not be indistinguishable from a day with no data.

Two supporting details worth carrying, neither of which changes the verdict:
- "missing= []" is weaker evidence than they present it as. loadSymbolAll hardcodes `return { rows, missing: [], cachedMonthCount: list.length }` at lib/pipeline.js:124 — that array can never be non-empty on the all-loaded path, whatever happened. The real tell is the silent 744 -> 720.
- The lost day is not smoothed into fake candles: forwardFill's maxGapHours=3 (lib/dataset.js:68) refuses a 24-hour gap, and I measured ffFills=0 in every corrupt case. That part of the design works. But its `fills` counter has no consumer at all — the only production caller, lib/bracketwork.js:68, takes `.map` and drops `.fills` on the floor — so a sub-4-hour loss would be invented over and counted nowhere.

Two corrections. One shaves the mechanism down; the other says the report is UNDER-stated, and the second matters much more.

1) WRONG, and it should be dropped: "c1 and c2 ... flow into pnlAt and into any report that reads them." Nothing reads chunk.c1/chunk.c2. `grep -rn "c1" --include=*.js --include=*.html . --exclude-dir=node_modules` returns only lib/dataset.js itself (lines 205/211/218/222/224/227/231, where they are produced) and test fixtures — no consumer in lib/, server.js, lib/live/, or public/. pnlAt is never handed chunk.c1; lib/pipeline.js:44 calls `pnlAt(call, entryC.open, exitC.open)` straight off the candle map. And pnlAt is immune anyway, because it only divides:
  pnlAt(1, "100.5", "103.2") = 2.436567164179099    numeric: 2.436567164179099
So the string-typed c1/c2 on the chunk record is a real symptom and a good detector, but it is inert on its own. The live damage in the reported run is the one zeroed feature.

2) UNDER-STATED, and this is the real finding: the report only ran geometry daily-1d, where `(c2 - c1) / c1` coerces and the labels survive. Under `weekly-8d` the labels do NOT survive — they are silently fabricated. That geometry's label path goes through lib/dataset.js:124, `for (const c of candles) sum += c.open + c.high + c.low + c.close;`, which concatenates the same way features.js:116 does. Direct check:
  meanOHLC numbers = 102.625
  meanOHLC strings = NaN
  scoreDiff(NaN, 0.02) = -1
`scoreDiff` (dataset.js) does `if (Math.abs(diffFrac) < dormantFrac) return 0; return diffFrac > 0 ? 1 : -1;` — `Math.abs(NaN) < x` is false and `NaN > 0` is false, so every NaN falls out of the bottom as a clean, confident -1. Same March-as-strings cache, geometry weekly-8d (t3.js):
  weekly-8d CONTROL      {"chunks":25,"up":3,"down":4,"flat":18,"nanDiff":0,"maxAbsDiffPct":3.446890800717242}
  weekly-8d STRING MARCH {"chunks":25,"up":3,"down":8,"flat":14,"nanDiff":4,"maxAbsDiffPct":3.446890800717242}
  label flips: 4 [
    '2024-02-26 0 -> -1 (c1=NaN diffPct=NaN)',
    '2024-03-04 0 -> -1 (c1=NaN diffPct=NaN)',
    '2024-03-11 0 -> -1 (c1=NaN diffPct=NaN)',
    '2024-03-18 0 -> -1 (c1=NaN diffPct=NaN)'

Four chunks that were "stand aside" become confident SHORT training labels manufactured out of NaN, and maxAbsDiffPct does not budge (3.446890800717242 both runs) because `Math.abs(NaN) || 0` collapses to 0 — the summary statistic a reviewer would glance at is the one thing that stays reassuring. That is the project's own archetype: not a crash, a plausible wrong answer. A corrupted training label outranks a zeroed feature.

This is reachable, not academic: `weekly-8d` is a user-selectable chunk shape — public/construct.js:448 renders `<option value="weekly-8d">Weekly 8-day</option>` in the `chunk shape` select. lib/batch.js:678 and :1974 refuse weekly-8d for ACTIVATION and History Tuning only; nothing stops it being swept and trained on.

The three read paths should apply the same row filter parseKlineCsv already applies. Caveat on reachability of string prices specifically: the only in-app writers to data/cache are binance.js (post-parseKlineCsv, always numeric) and lib/planted.js:188 (generated numerics), so a string-priced cache file arrives by hand-edit, restore, or an external tool — but the missing validation is real for every malformed-row class, not just strings.
