confirmed.correction:
The finding is real. Three things in it are wrong, and all three make it sound smaller than it is.

**1. The severity is backwards. This is the WORST of the three price cases, not the mildest.** The report says it is "lower-consequence than the zero/negative case". The opposite is true: 1e308 is the only one of the three that overflows to Infinity downstream, and overflow is what carries the damage OUT of the poisoned chunk into every other chunk.

Features are z-scored at lib/bracket.js:507-509 via standardizeFit/standardizeApply in lib/logreg.js. I fed the real 181-chunk matrix through that path (run.js above):

  [control] non-finite std cols: 0 []
  [control] one-row-dominated columns: 0 []
  [poison]  non-finite std cols: 1 [ 'trade_max_runup std=Infinity mean=5.3593183754911464e+303' ]
  [poison]  columns that are ALL ZERO after z-scoring: 5 [ 'trade_max_runup', 'trade_dayvol_cv', 'trade_dayvol_last_ratio', 'comp_dayvol_cv', 'comp_dayvol_last_ratio' ]   (control had the same 4 minus trade_max_runup)
  [poison]  one-row-dominated columns: 8 [ 'trade_hourly_vol top|z|=13.42 next=0.0746', 'trade_vol_shift top|z|=9.24 next=1.3586', 'trade_trend_slope top|z|=13.38 next=0.1803', 'trade_trend_accel top|z|=13.42 next=0.0759', 'trade_max_drawdown top|z|=12.99 next=0.3370', 'trade_range top|z|=13.42 next=0.0869', 'rel_vol_log top|z|=13.41 next=0.1024', 'ret_correlation top|z|=13.42 next=0.0820' ]
  [poison]  non-finite values in Z matrix: 0

In standardizeFit the squared deviation (9.7e305)^2 overflows, so std becomes Infinity; standardizeApply then divides every row by Infinity and `trade_max_runup` comes out exactly 0 for ALL 181 chunks. A feature is silently deleted from the model. Eight more columns are taken over by the single poisoned row (|z| ~13 against a next-largest of ~0.08). And there is not one NaN or Infinity left in the matrix to notice — this is precisely the project's "plausible wrong answer" failure, at dataset scale, from one hour. Zero and negative prices stay finite and damage only their own chunk's z-scores.

**2. It also corrupts the persisted model, and training and reload then disagree.** lib/bracket.js:516 saves `std: Array.from(scaler.std)`; `Infinity` JSON-serializes to `null`; lib/bracket.js:559 then computes `z[j] = (x[j] - saved.mean[j]) / saved.std[j]`. Measured on a clean, untouched chunk (run2.js):

  in-memory std   = Infinity    after JSON round trip = null
  clean chunk raw trade_max_runup = 0.030100169660678616
  z used at TRAINING time   = -0
  z from the RELOADED model = -Infinity
  agree? false

The comment at lib/bracket.js:550-553 says a test exists to catch exactly this round-trip disagreement. It is reachable through cached data, not code.

**3. "Labels/chunk count unchanged" is an artifact of the hour that was picked, not a property of the attack.** Hour 300 is 2024-03-13T12:00Z, and under daily-1d (entryOffsetH 25, exitOffsetH 42 in lib/dataset.js:33) that is neither the entry nor the exit candle. Move the same 1e308 onto the hours that are (run3.js):

  --- 1e308 at 2024-03-14T01:00:00.000Z (the entry open) ---
    chunk 2024-03-13  c1 99.775287 -> 1e+308   diffPct -2.414808388373774 -> -100   label -1 -> -1   kept in dataset? yes; diffPct finite? true
  --- 1e308 at 2024-03-14T18:00:00.000Z (the exit open) ---
    chunk 2024-03-13  c2 97.365905 -> 1e+308   diffPct -2.414808388373774 -> 1.0022521909658852e+308   label -1 -> 1   kept in dataset? yes; diffPct finite? true
    tally 181 chunks, up 66 / down 62 / flat 53   (control: up 65 / down 63 / flat 53)

One poisoned hour manufactures a training label — a chunk that really fell 2.4% is taught to the model as "up". The chunk is not dropped and diffPct is finite, so nothing anywhere refuses it.

**4. The proposed fix would not have caught this on its own.** "A sanity band on cached prices applied at read time" is worth having, but the reason 1e308 escapes is that finiteness is checked on inputs only and never on OUTPUTS — the report's own evidence has a 9.7e+305 sailing past `Number.isFinite` at lib/features.js:69. Two cheaper checks each catch it independently: (a) a magnitude band on the emitted feature values, which is well-defined here because the file's own comment at lib/features.js:62-64 states "Everything is scale-free (returns, ratios) so chunks at $20 and chunks at $700 describe the same shapes with the same numbers" — 9.7e+305 is not a ratio; (b) a non-finite/degenerate-large guard in standardizeFit, which already has the mirror case at lib/logreg.js:41-42 (`if (std[j] < 1e-12) std[j] = 1;`) and no handler for std blowing up.

**5. One part of the report holds up.** "Nothing in the product looks at a feature vector" is correct — I checked: `c.x` appears only at lib/bracket.js:60, 74, 484, 486; no route in server.js or lib/live/routes.js returns feature values, and public/trade.html surfaces only feature names and counts (lib/live/anatomy.js:74, 83). So the absurd magnitude is genuinely invisible. That is an argument for raising the severity, not lowering it.

No repository file was modified (`git status --porcelain` clean); all work was in /tmp scratch dirs, and no server was started.

The finding stands. Three corrections, all making it worse or sharper than written.

1) SEVERITY IS UNDERSTATED — this is a collision, not a dangling reference. The report says the setup ends up "pointing at a sub-account reference that does not exist." The real outcome is worse: every setup whose "Save routing" is pressed converges on the SAME literal string "set". I pressed it once on each of two setups and observed both on disk:
    mine-1     state=draft  keyRef='set'
    mine-live  state=live   keyRef='set'
That is precisely the shared-sub-account condition the mechanism exists to prevent. lib/live/setups.js:257-262 states that any two setups sharing one isolated-margin sub-account "mingle their balance AND borrow pool, so multi-day short interest pools onto whichever leg closes last and cross-contaminates the other setup's realized." A nonexistent reference would at least fail loudly at the executor; two live books resolving to one identical reference is the silent-wrong-number failure. I grepped for any distinctness enforcement — there is none anywhere in the codebase; liveGateErrors checks only non-emptiness, so the collision clears every gate.

2) IT HITS SETUPS ALREADY TRADING, not just live-eligible ones. The report says the setup "stays live-eligible." I tested the stronger case: I transitioned mine-live to state 'live' first, then pressed the button with the execution target dropdown set to mx-1. Result on disk: state live keyRef 'set' target 'mx-1'. The guard written specifically to catch this — the touchesRouting re-check at lib/live/setups.js:227-235, which re-runs liveGateErrors on a paper/live/stopped setup precisely because updateSetup can mutate keyRef — ran, evaluated "set".trim() as truthy, and waved it through with ok:true. So the defence built for this exact hazard is the thing that certifies the corruption. Note also that on a 'draft' setup the gate does not run at all (draft is excluded from that branch), so drafts are corrupted with no check whatsoever.

3) THE LOSS IS UNRECOVERABLE AND UNDETECTABLE THROUGH THE INTERFACE. Both read paths mask: routes.js:64 for the detail, and summarize() at routes.js:29 (keyRef: s.keyRef ? 'set' : null) for the list. I confirmed no route returns a raw keyRef, and the catalog does not leak it. The Key tile at trade.html:545 is `s.keyRef?'set':'none'` with class 'pos' (.pos{color:var(--pos)} at trade.html:34) — so after the overwrite the tile still reads "set" in the positive colour, byte-identical to before. A second press is byte-identical too. The consequence: the owner cannot discover that anything was lost, and cannot read back what the value used to be — the true reference is gone from the system entirely, recoverable only from the exchange or the owner's own records.

One caveat on the EXPECTED as written. "Save routing must omit keyRef when the box still holds the sentinel" is a workable patch but carries its own trap: a real key whose value happened to be the string "set" would become unsettable, and the owner still gets no way to tell a correctly-set key from a wrong one. The cleaner statement of the expectation is the report's first branch — a masked read value must never be the seed for an editable write control. Reads and writes of keyRef should not share a field at all. (Flagging only; per RULE ZERO I have made no change — no repository file was edited.)

The defect is real but three parts of the write-up are wrong or imprecise, and two things are worse than reported.

CORRECTION 1 - the header is not contradicted. I verified median([]) === null is true. The header's literal promise (an empty list returns null, not NaN) is kept. What the NaN case breaks is the header's stated RATIONALE - that a caller writing this into a report can tell "not available" from a number - not its stated behaviour. "Contradicting its own header" overstates it.

CORRECTION 2 - "order-dependent" is the wrong diagnosis of the live path. At lib/batch.js:1889 the argument is Object.values(doc.nullTest.samples), and samples is keyed by integer shiftIndex. JS enumerates integer-like keys in ascending numeric order, so parallel lane arrival order never reaches the sort. I banked samples in scrambled arrival order [7,3,11,1,9,5,2,10,4,8,6] and Object.values still came out 1,2,...,11. Same fixed array run 1000 times gives one answer ('NaN'). So this is NOT run-to-run nondeterminism; the answer is decided by WHICH rotation index went bad. A fixer who reads "order-dependent" as a lane-scheduling race will chase the wrong thing.

CORRECTION 3 - reachability is asserted, not shown, and I could not show it either. NaN candles are dropped at ingest: lib/binance.js:96, if (!(open > 0 && high > 0 && low > 0 && close > 0)) continue - NaN fails that test and the row never enters. The other obvious NaN source, the fee, is clamped at lib/batch.js:1231-1232: Number(params.feePerLeg) >= 0 ? Number(...) : REAL_FEE_PER_LEG, so a NaN fee falls back to the constant. So the claim "one NaN replicate silently shifts the reported null distribution" is conditional on a NaN source neither of us exhibited. Rank this as a latent invariant hole in a shared helper, not a wrong number currently reachable on screen.

ADDITION A - the case the report treats as loud is silent too. JSON.stringify({medianBestPnl: NaN}) yields {"medianBestPnl":null} (verified). The batch doc is persisted and served as JSON, so when the NaN lands mid-list and median returns NaN, what is written and shipped is null - the exact sentinel the header reserves for "no data". So BOTH failure modes are silent: either a plausible wrong number, or a false "not available". The distinguishability the header is arguing for collapses in both directions, which strengthens the finding.

ADDITION B - the more dangerous number is the sibling line, and fixing median alone will not fix it. lib/batch.js:1888 computes exceedSearch = vals.filter(x => x.best >= sel.pnl).length / vals.length. A NaN sample counts in the denominator and can never count in the numerator, so it biases the figure toward significance. Measured with 11 rotations of which 3 exceed a real pnl of 900: clean {"exceedSearch":0.2727272727272727}, one exceeding rotation turned NaN {"exceedSearch":0.18181818181818182}. It is structurally incapable of emitting a non-positive price.
   So reaching this requires an out-of-band writer with write access to data/cache — at which point that writer could equally rewrite lib/paper.js. This is a validation asymmetry / defence-in-depth gap, NOT a reachable defect. That is a real downgrade from how it reads.

2. "WINS THE CELL SELECTION" IS CORRECT — I tried to refute this and failed. lib/plateau.js:28 `clears()` does guard (`Number.isFinite(row.pnl) && row.pnl > 0 && ...`), which initially looked like a refutation, but that guards REGION MEMBERSHIP only. There is no in-app producer of a torn day file. The catch does still swallow EACCES / ENOSPC-truncated files and monthFromDayFiles then returns a short month with no signal — that part is real — but "torn read" specifically is a hazard the code already designed out.

FOUND WHILE ATTACKING (same surface, strictly more reachable than the zero-price case, and not reported): the `Array.isArray(cached)` check accepts an EMPTY array as a complete month. In the scratch copy I wrote `[]` into BTCUSDT-1h-2024-05.json:
